source.title: Enhancing Gradient Variance and Differential Privacy in Quantum Federated Learning
source.citation: Duc T. T. Phan et al., 2025
source.authors: Duc T. T. Phan; Minh-Duong Nguyen; Quoc-Viet Pham; Hui-Long Pi

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses the proposed link between gradient variance, sharp minima, and generalization, but its own experiments do not measure the training–test gap or test that link. Its experiments concern federated privacy and classification accuracy.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy and training-accuracy curves for its QFL method and baselines, but these do not test any listed version: it does not compare training and test error, random-label memorization with natural-label generalization, or the listed interventions and gap measures. It argues that adaptive noise can help with gradient variance and sharp minima, without measuring generalization gaps.
record.test_reason: The study discusses sharp minima and generalization as motivation, but its own results evaluate quantum federated learning, privacy, convergence, and classification accuracy. It tests none of V1–V8. Its sharp-minimizer argument concerns optimization stagnation, not whether magnitude-aware sharpness ranks training–test gaps. The record's tests/T5 classification is incorrect.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately captures the authors' conclusion: they present ADP-QFL as providing client-level privacy while improving the trade-off among accuracy, convergence, and communication efficiency, and argue that adaptive noise mitigates gradient-variance-related stagnation. They report no measured training–test gap. Their efficiency claim is qualified by longer CIFAR-10 training times than FedBN and FedRep.
record.recipe_differences: Quantum federated learning with client-level differential privacy, adaptive noise, model estimation, and classification-accuracy evaluation; it does not use the original methods or measures in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported accuracy varies with dataset, privacy budget, and participating-client fraction; these experiments do not measure the claimed training–test gap.

fits_no_version.finding: Table IV reports ADP-QFL test accuracies of 98.47% on MNIST and 83.85% on CIFAR-10; Table VI compares its test accuracy with methods lacking model estimation or using classical private federated learning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive noise and model estimation can improve classification utility in the tested private quantum federated learning setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Section V.C and Corollaries 1–3 argue that adaptive noise can counter reduced gradient variance and sharp-minimizer stagnation. They provide no measured sharpness–generalization-gap relationship.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive noise can mitigate optimization stagnation attributed to reduced quantum gradient variance under the paper's theoretical setup.

record.problems: No experiment measures training error against test error or evaluates generalization-gap claims. Privacy-budget results are described partly through figures, and the reported training-accuracy curves do not establish test performance for those conditions.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible result rows. Reported classification accuracies, training-time comparisons, and convergence curves concern federated privacy and utility, not the behaviors measured by the listed versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance compared with natural-label training using the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets; Adam is used without an optimizer comparison.
Large versus small minibatches under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations to the training recipe. Varying participating clients does not establish this comparison.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and removal of dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Identification and removal of memorized examples followed by retraining, compared with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: Leaving the result rows empty is appropriate for these claim versions. Ordinary held-out accuracy does not alone test them; several versions require specific interventions rather than a training–test-gap measurement.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training, memorization-capacity comparison, or natural-label generalization comparison.
No width sweep or test-error evaluation around or beyond interpolation.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Uses Adam but does not compare optimizers or assess a training–test gap.
No batch-size sweep or large-batch generalization-gap comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measure or comparison with generalization gaps.
No memorized-example identification, removal, or retraining comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The paper discusses sharp minima and generalization as motivation but neither tests nor uses a cataloged claim version as a tool.

tranche.reason: Sections V–VII analyze quantum federated learning convergence, privacy, accuracy, and communication costs. None tests V1–V8; the sharp-minimizer argument concerns optimization stagnation rather than magnitude-aware sharpness tracking generalization gaps.

source_check.notes: No rows, synthesis statements, or verdicts are listed. Training and test accuracy appear, but no measured training–test gap or comparison testing V1–V8 is reported.
